title_tag: Anthropic soars, but it may soon be back, cap in hand —— 英国《经济学人》外刊讲解第1235天
h1: Anthropic soars, but it may soon be back, cap in hand
category: 英国《经济学人》外刊讲解 第1235天

headline.en_html: The biggest IPO of all time is just a start

paragraphs.en_html: And so it was that a bunch of AI nerds on November 19th pulled off the biggest stock-market listing of all time. Anthropic, a San Francisco-based company that is not even six years old, raised $107bn in an initial public offering (IPO) that included a $26bn private share sale to tech-giant backers such as Google and Nvidia. An initial surge in Anthropic’s share price briefly pushed its value above $2trn. At the close of its first day of trading it was off its highs but still up over 17%.

The financial feat, impressive as it is, will not be the last time Anthropic comes to the capital markets with palms outstretched. It will need plenty of funding to stay ahead in the race to build frontier AI, where it faces competition from arch-rival OpenAI and a growing array of open-source model makers. Its new investors, excited as they are to buy shares in the first pure-play AI lab to tap the public markets, may find themselves asked to open their wallets again in the future.

The IPO gives Anthropic a big cushion. Ahead of the listing, the company had almost $132bn in cash and short-term investments. It now has more than $230bn, surpassing more traditional tech giants with the exception of Google’s parent company, Alphabet, which had $265bn at the end of the most recent quarter.

Anthropic will probably need even more to build what Dario Amodei, its boss, calls a “country of geniuses in a data centre”—ie, superintelligence capable of surpassing humans in almost every realm that requires brainpower. It has committed to spending $900bn on computing power until 2045, with about half of that due by the end of 2030. That requires making bold assumptions: while it is hard to predict how aggressively customers will adopt AI in coming years, some computing providers require large spending commitments more than a year in advance. Mr Amodei recently called this conundrum Anthropic’s “deepest business dilemma”.

Its rocketing performance could help resolve the dilemma. As long as revenue grows by more than 20% annually through 2035, Anthropic should be able to cover its computing commitments, reckons William Blair, a bank. Anthropic has grown considerably faster than that. It also needs to generate sustainable profits. It briefly made an operating profit of nearly $1bn in the second quarter before swinging to a loss in the following three-month period.

In addition, the model maker has admitted it may need other sources of funding to pay for the AI chips it uses to train and run new versions of its Claude bot. In the run-up to the IPO, it told potential investors that its ability to get enough computing power “is directly linked to our ability to access capital on favourable terms”. Being a public company should make the task easier. Until now, Anthropic has turned to off-balance-sheet deals such as that last month with Broadcom, a chip designer, and Blackstone, among other financial firms, to raise $63bn for server purchases.

Its menu of options may include more traditional debt offerings. It was given a BB+ credit rating, one notch below investment grade, by Kroll Bond Rating Agency in June before a $35bn chip financing deal with Apollo Global Management, an investment firm. Investors expect Anthropic to push for an investment-grade rating now that its financial performance is public, allowing it to borrow more cheaply.

Keeping the funding taps open will be easier if sentiment towards AI strengthens. That is far from assured. Nvidia, the chipmaker at the centre of the AI boom, lost its boss, Jensen Huang, last week, and markets have yet to steady. Politics is turning, too. In this month’s midterm elections voters backed dozens of ballot measures restricting AI, and an anti-data-centre backlash may have helped Democrats sweep to victory. Their incoming leaders have promised moratoriums on the very facilities that Anthropic’s computing commitments depend on. Elizabeth Warren, a Democratic senator, has warned of threats to Americans’ retirements if the IPO goes awry. The White House has so far waved away talk of a bubble, and Donald Trump, who likens data centres to “GOLD”, will resist a crackdown. Yet a Congress turned hostile could raise the price of both capital and concrete. Anthropic’s own prospectus concedes that AI may advance faster than oversight can keep up.

Anthropic’s record-breaking stock-market debut suggests Wall Street is excited to spread its bets from AI hardware and cloud-computing firms to model makers. But despite its first-day rally, broader share-price indices continued to decline. For all the Anthropic fever, the stock market’s mood swings about AI remain as volatile as ever. ■
